introduction-hope-is-not-a-strategy.core: In distributed systems some dependency is always failing. Resilient code assumes that and contains it: retry wisely, stop calling dead services and isolate resources.

first_principles.problem: A delivery app with four dependencies fails completely whenever any one of them hiccups.
truths: The probability that something fails rises with the number of dependencies.
derivation: Expect **transient failures** and retry with backoff and jitter.
Expect **sustained outages** and use a circuit breaker.

analogy.title: Defensive driving
analogy.story: Assume other drivers will make mistakes, and leave space and escape routes.
analogy.breaks: Resilience patterns add complexity and need tests, including chaos testing.

steps.label: Insight
steps.detail: Reliability has to be designed in; it doesn't emerge on its own.

check.q: Why do more dependencies lower overall availability?
check.a: Availabilities multiply, so each extra dependency adds another chance of failure.

pattern-1-exponential-backoff-with-jitte.core: Retry failed calls after exponentially growing delays (1s, 2s, 4s…) plus random jitter, so clients spread out instead of stampeding a recovering service.

first_principles.problem: 1,000 clients fail together and all retry at exactly the same moment, knocking the database over again: a thundering herd.
truths: Transient failures often clear in seconds.
derivation: **Cap** the delay and the number of attempts.
Retry only **idempotent** operations and retryable errors.

analogy.title: A crowd leaving through one door
analogy.story: If everyone surges at once, nobody gets out. Staggered exits flow smoothly.
analogy.breaks: Retries amplify load during real outages, so pair them with a circuit breaker and retry budgets.

example.title: A retry loop with full jitter

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Retries spread smoothly over time, so the service recovers.

example.outcome: transient failures are absorbed without a stampede.

check.a: It de-synchronises clients so their retries don't arrive at the same instant.

pattern-2-the-circuit-breaker.core: A circuit breaker tracks failures to a dependency. After a threshold it 'opens' and fails fast without calling, then after a cooldown lets a test call through (half-open) to see whether the dependency has recovered.

first_principles.problem: Retrying a service that's been down for 5 minutes wastes threads, adds latency and piles load onto it while it tries to recover.
truths: You need a way to detect recovery.
derivation: **Closed**: calls flow and failures are counted.
**Open**: fail immediately, perhaps with a fallback.
**Half-open**: after a timeout, allow a probe.
Probe succeeds → close; fails → open again.

analogy.title: A household circuit breaker
analogy.story: When the wiring overloads, it trips to prevent a fire. You reset it once the fault is fixed.
analogy.breaks: Choosing thresholds is hard: too sensitive flaps, too lax doesn't protect.

example.title: A recommendations service outage

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Pages load fast with fallback content instead of timing out.

example.outcome: outages degrade gracefully and recovery is detected automatically.

check.q: What happens in the half-open state?
check.a: A limited number of trial calls go through to test whether the dependency has recovered.

pattern-3-the-bulkhead.core: A bulkhead partitions resources (thread pools, connection pools, concurrency limits) per dependency or tenant, so one slow dependency can't exhaust everything and sink the whole service.

first_principles.problem: One slow downstream API ties up all 200 worker threads, and every other endpoint, healthy ones included, stops responding.
truths: Resources are finite and shared by default.
derivation: Give each dependency its **own pool or semaphore**.
When a partition is full, **reject fast** instead of queuing forever.

analogy.title: Watertight compartments in a ship
analogy.story: If one compartment floods, the doors hold and the ship stays afloat.
analogy.breaks: Too many small partitions waste capacity, so balance isolation against utilisation.

example.title: Separate pools for payments and reviews

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Reviews hang, but checkout keeps working.

code.text:
pay_sem = asyncio.Semaphore(50)
rev_sem = asyncio.Semaphore(10)
async def get_reviews():
    if rev_sem.locked(): return []   # degrade
    async with rev_sem: return await reviews_api()

example.outcome: one failure can't consume every resource.

check.q: What failure does a bulkhead prevent?
check.a: One slow dependency exhausting shared resources and taking down unrelated functionality.
